title: Differentiability Implies Continuity
one_liner: Theorem 2.2.3 states that if a function $f$ is differentiable at a point $x_0$, then $f$ is also continuous at that point $x_0$.
content: Theorem 2.2.3 states that if a function $f$ is differentiable at $x_{0}$, then $f$ is continuous at $x_{0}$.
motivation_md: This theorem establishes a fundamental relationship between two core concepts in calculus: differentiability and continuity. It helps us understand that the existence of a well-defined tangent line (differentiability) at a point implies the function must not have any breaks or jumps (continuity) at that same point.
recap_md: - Differentiability at a point implies continuity at that point.

title: Continuity Does Not Imply Differentiability
one_liner: The converse of Theorem 2.2.3 is false: a function can be continuous at a point but not differentiable there, such as at corner points like $f(x)=|x|$ at $x=0$.
content: The converse of Theorem 2.2.3 is false; that is, a function may be continuous at a point but not differentiable at that point. This situation occurs, for example, at corner points of continuous functions. For instance, the function $f(x)=|x|$ is continuous at $x=0$ but is not differentiable there, as shown in Example 6.
motivation_md: It's crucial to understand that while differentiability implies continuity, the reverse is not true. This concept highlights that a function can be unbroken (continuous) but still lack a unique tangent line (not differentiable) at certain points, which is important for correctly analyzing function behavior.
recap_md: - Continuity at a point does not guarantee differentiability at that point.

title: Historical Significance of Differentiability and Continuity
one_liner: The relationship between continuity and differentiability held great historical significance, challenging early mathematicians' geometric intuition and leading to discoveries of functions continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere.
content: The relationship between continuity and differentiability was of great historical significance in the development of calculus. In the early nineteenth century, mathematicians believed that if a continuous function had many points of nondifferentiability, these points would have to be separated from one another and joined by smooth curve segments, much like the tips of a sawblade (Figure 2.2.12). This misconception was corrected by a series of discoveries beginning in 1834. That year, Bernhard Bolzano, a Bohemian priest, philosopher, and mathematician, discovered a procedure for constructing a continuous function that is not differentiable at any point. Later, in 1860, the German mathematician Karl Weierstrass produced the first formula for such a function. The graphs of these functions are impossible to draw because the corners are so numerous that any segment of the curve, when suitably enlarged, reveals even more corners. The discovery of these functions was important because it made mathematicians distrustful of their geometric intuition and more reliant on precise mathematical proof. Recently, such functions have begun to play a fundamental role in the study of geometric objects called fractals, which have revealed an order to natural phenomena previously dismissed as random and chaotic.
motivation_md: Understanding the historical development of calculus reveals how mathematicians' intuition was refined by rigorous proof. The discovery of functions that are continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere fundamentally changed how functions were perceived, emphasizing the need for formal definitions over visual assumptions and paving the way for new mathematical fields like fractals.
recap_md: - Early mathematicians incorrectly assumed continuous functions with many non-differentiable points would still have smooth segments.

title: One-Sided Derivatives (Left-Hand and Right-Hand)
one_liner: One-sided derivatives, $f_{-}^{\prime}(x)$ and $f_{+}^{\prime}(x)$, are defined as limits from the left and right, respectively, to handle differentiability at interval endpoints.
content: If a function $f$ is defined on a closed interval $[a, b]$ but not outside that interval, then $f^{\prime}$ is not defined at the endpoints of the interval because derivatives are two-sided limits. To address this, we define left-hand derivatives and right-hand derivatives as follows:$$f_{-}^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0^{-}} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \quad \text { and } \quad f_{+}^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$$These are called one-sided derivatives. Geometrically, $f_{-}^{\prime}(x)$ represents the limit of the slopes of the secant lines as $x$ is approached from the left, and $f_{+}^{\prime}(x)$ is the limit of the slopes of the secant lines as $x$ is approached from the right. [FIGURE:037488adaedba825 | A graph displays a continuous, wavy blue curve labeled $y=f(x)$ above a horizontal axis. At $x=a$, a dashed vertical line extends from the axis to a point on the curve. A purple line segment, tangent...]
motivation_md: One-sided derivatives are essential for analyzing the differentiability of functions at the endpoints of closed intervals or at points where the function's behavior changes abruptly, like corners. They allow us to extend the concept of a derivative to situations where a full two-sided limit does not exist or is not applicable.
recap_md: - The left-hand derivative $f_{-}^{\prime}(x)$ uses a limit as $h \rightarrow 0^{-}$.

title: Notation for the Derivative (dy/dx)
one_liner: The symbol $dy/dx$ should be regarded as a single notation for the derivative, not a ratio, though $dy$ and $dx$ will later have specific meanings.
content: Later, the symbols $d y$ and $d x$ will be given specific meanings. However, for the time being, do not regard $d y / d x$ as a ratio, but rather as a single symbol denoting the derivative. For a closed interval $[a, b]$, we will understand the derivative at the left endpoint to be $f_{+}^{\prime}(a)$ and at the right endpoint to be $f_{-}^{\prime}(b)$ (Figure 2.2.13).
motivation_md: Understanding derivative notation is fundamental for communicating mathematical ideas effectively. This concept clarifies that $dy/dx$ is initially a single symbol for the derivative, preventing premature assumptions about it being a fraction, which is crucial for building a solid foundation in calculus.
recap_md: - Treat $dy/dx$ as a single symbol for the derivative, not a ratio, for now.

title: Differentiable on an Interval
one_liner: A function is differentiable on an interval if it is differentiable at all interior points and has the appropriate one-sided derivative at any included endpoints.
content: In general, we will say that $f$ is differentiable on an interval of the form $[a, b],[a,+\infty)$, $(-\infty, b],[a, b)$, or $(a, b]$ if it is differentiable at all points inside the interval and the appropriate one-sided derivative exists at each included endpoint.
motivation_md: This definition extends the concept of differentiability from a single point to an entire interval, which is essential for analyzing the behavior of functions over a range. It clarifies how to handle endpoints using one-sided derivatives, ensuring a consistent understanding of differentiability across different types of intervals.
recap_md: - A function is differentiable on an interval if it's differentiable at all interior points.

title: Continuity and One-Sided Derivatives
one_liner: A function $f$ is continuous from the left (or right) at points where its left-hand (or right-hand) derivative exists.
content: It can be proved that a function $f$ is continuous from the left at those points where the left-hand derivative exists and is continuous from the right at those points where the right-hand derivative exists.
motivation_md: This idea connects one-sided differentiability with one-sided continuity, providing a deeper understanding of function behavior at specific points, especially endpoints or points of discontinuity. It reinforces the relationship between differentiability and continuity, even in a directional sense.
recap_md: - Existence of a left-hand derivative implies continuity from the left.

title: Other Derivative Notations
one_liner: Differentiation is an operation that associates a function $f'$ with $f$, commonly denoted by various symbols like $d/dx[f(x)]$, $D_x[f(x)]$, $y'(x)$, or $dy/dx$.
content: The process of finding a derivative is called differentiation. You can think of differentiation as an operation on functions that associates a function $f^{\prime}$ with a function $f$. When the independent variable is $x$, the differentiation operation is also commonly denoted by$$f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)] \quad \text { or } \quad f^{\prime}(x)=D_{x}[f(x)]$$In the case where there is a dependent variable $y=f(x)$, the derivative is also commonly denoted by$$f^{\prime}(x)=y^{\prime}(x) \quad \text { or } \quad f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{d y}{d x}$$With the above notations, the value of the derivative at a point $x_{0}$ can be expressed as$$f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=\left.\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]\right|_{x=x_{0}}, \quad f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=\left.D_{x}[f(x)]\right|_{x=x_{0}}, \quad f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=y^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right), \quad f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=\left.\frac{d y}{d x}\right|_{x=x_{0}}$$
motivation_md: Calculus uses several notations for derivatives, each with its own advantages in different contexts. Familiarity with these various forms is crucial for reading, writing, and understanding mathematical expressions in calculus, ensuring clear communication and flexibility in problem-solving.
recap_md: - Differentiation is an operation that maps a function to its derivative.

title: Continuity at a point
one_liner: A function $f$ is continuous at $x=c$ if $f(c)$ is defined, the limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $c$ exists, and these two values are equal.
content: A function $f$ is said to be continuous at $ oldsymbol{x}= oldsymbol{c}$ provided the following three conditions are satisfied: 1. $f(c)$ is defined. 2. $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ exists. 3. $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)=f(c)$.
motivation_md: The concept of continuity at a point is fundamental in calculus, describing functions that have no abrupt changes, breaks, or holes at a specific point. It ensures that the function's value at that point matches its limiting behavior.
recap_md: - A function $f$ is continuous at $c$ if $f(c)$ is defined. - The limit of $f(x)$ as $x \rightarrow c$ must exist. - The limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ must equal $f(c)$.

title: Jump discontinuity
one_liner: A function has a jump discontinuity at $c$ if its one-sided limits as $x$ approaches $c$ both exist but are not equal.
content: If one or more of the conditions for continuity fails to hold, then $f$ has a discontinuity at $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{c}$. A function has a jump discontinuity at $c$ if the one-sided limits of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $c$ both exist but are not equal. This means that $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ does not exist, violating the second condition of continuity.
motivation_md: Classifying different types of discontinuities helps us understand the specific ways a function can fail to be continuous. A jump discontinuity signifies an abrupt, finite change in the function's value at a point, often seen in piecewise functions.
recap_md: - A jump discontinuity occurs when the left-hand and right-hand limits at a point exist. - However, these one-sided limits are not equal. - Consequently, the overall limit at that point does not exist.

title: Infinite discontinuity
one_liner: A function has an infinite discontinuity at $c$ if its one-sided limits as $x$ approaches $c$ are infinite.
content: If one or more of the conditions for continuity fails to hold, then $f$ has a discontinuity at $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{c}$. A function has an infinite discontinuity at $c$ if its one-sided limits as $x$ approaches $c$ are infinite. This means that $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ does not exist, violating the second condition of continuity.
motivation_md: Understanding infinite discontinuities is crucial for identifying vertical asymptotes and points where a function's value grows without bound. This type of discontinuity indicates a fundamental break in the function's graph.
recap_md: - An infinite discontinuity occurs when one or both one-sided limits at a point are infinite. - This implies the overall limit at that point does not exist. - Such discontinuities are often associated with vertical asymptotes.

title: Removable discontinuity
one_liner: A function has a removable discontinuity at $c$ if $f(c)$ is defined and $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ exists, but these two values are not equal.
content: If one or more of the conditions for continuity fails to hold, then $f$ has a discontinuity at $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{c}$. A function has a removable discontinuity at $c$ if the function is defined at $c$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ exists, but these two values are not equal. This violates the third condition of continuity. Discontinuities of this type are called "removable" because they can be eliminated by redefining the function at a single point.
motivation_md: Removable discontinuities are important because they represent 'holes' in a function's graph that can be 'filled' by redefining the function at a single point. This concept is key for simplifying rational functions and understanding their behavior.
recap_md: - A removable discontinuity occurs when $f(c)$ is defined and $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ exists. - However, $f(c) \neq \lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$. - This type of discontinuity can be 'removed' by redefining $f(c)$ to be equal to the limit.

title: Continuity in applications
one_liner: In real-world applications, discontinuities often signal the occurrence of important physical events, such as a sudden change in voltage or inventory.
content: In applications, discontinuities often signal the occurrence of important physical events. For example, a graph of voltage versus time for an underground cable that is accidentally cut at time $t=t_{0}$ will show a discontinuity as the voltage drops to zero. Another example is a graph of inventory versus time for a company that restocks its warehouse; discontinuities occur at the times when restocking happens.
motivation_md: Understanding continuity and discontinuity is vital for modeling real-world phenomena. Discontinuities in mathematical models often correspond to critical, abrupt changes or events in physical systems, allowing us to analyze and predict such occurrences.
recap_md: - Discontinuities in applied contexts often represent significant physical events. - Examples include sudden voltage drops when a cable is cut. - Another example is inventory jumps when a warehouse is restocked.

title: Continuity on an open interval
one_liner: A function $f$ is continuous on an open interval $(a, b)$ if it is continuous at every number within that interval.
content: If a function $f$ is continuous at each number in an open interval $(a, b)$, then we say that $f$ is continuous on $(\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b})$. This definition also applies to infinite open intervals of the form $(a,+\infty)$, $(-\infty, b)$, and $(-\infty,+\infty)$. In the special case where $f$ is continuous on $(-\infty,+\infty)$, we will say that $f$ is continuous everywhere.
motivation_md: Extending the concept of continuity from a single point to an entire interval allows for a broader analysis of function behavior. This is essential for understanding properties like differentiability and integrability over a range of values.
recap_md: - A function is continuous on an open interval if it is continuous at every point in that interval. - This definition applies to infinite open intervals like $(a, \infty)$ and $(-\infty, \infty)$. - If a function is continuous on $(-\infty, \infty)$, it is said to be continuous everywhere.

title: Continuity at endpoints
one_liner: Continuity at an interval's endpoint is defined by the function's value at that endpoint being equal to the appropriate one-sided limit.
content: Because the definition of continuity at a point (Definition 1.5.1) involves a two-sided limit, it does not generally apply at the endpoints of a closed interval $[a, b]$ or at the endpoint of intervals like $[a, b)$, $(a, b]$, $(-\infty, b]$, or $[a,+\infty)$. To address this, we define a function as continuous at an endpoint of an interval if its value at that endpoint is equal to the appropriate one-sided limit. For example, a function graphed in Figure 1.5.4 is continuous at the right endpoint of the interval $[a, b]$ if $\lim _{x \rightarrow b^{-}} f(x)=f(b)$, but it is not continuous at the left endpoint if $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x) \neq f(a)$.
motivation_md: The standard definition of continuity requires a two-sided limit, which isn't possible at an interval's edge. This concept provides a necessary extension, allowing us to define continuity for closed and half-open intervals, which is crucial for theorems like the Intermediate Value Theorem.
recap_md: - The two-sided limit in the definition of continuity does not apply at interval endpoints. - Continuity at an endpoint is defined using the appropriate one-sided limit. - For example, at a right endpoint $b$, continuity requires $\lim _{x \rightarrow b^{-}} f(x)=f(b)$.

title: Continuous from the left
one_liner: A function $f$ is continuous from the left at $c$ if the limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $c$ from the left equals $f(c)$.
content: In general, we will say a function $f$ is continuous from the left at $c$ if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{-}} f(x)=f(c)$.
motivation_md: Defining continuity from the left (or right) is essential for precisely describing function behavior at endpoints of intervals or at points where a function might be piecewise defined. It allows for a more nuanced understanding of continuity where a full two-sided limit might not exist or be applicable.
recap_md: - A function $f$ is continuous from the left at $c$ if the left-hand limit exists. - This left-hand limit must be equal to the function's value at $c$. - The condition is $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{-}} f(x)=f(c)$.

title: Strategy for Finding Limits Algebraically
one_liner: Our strategy for finding limits algebraically involves first obtaining limits of simple functions, then using theorems to build limits of more complicated functions.
content: Our strategy for finding limits algebraically has two parts: First, we will obtain the limits of some simple functions. Then, we will develop a repertoire of theorems that will enable us to use the limits of those simple functions as building blocks for finding limits of more complicated functions.
motivation_md: To effectively evaluate limits, a systematic approach is necessary. This strategy provides a roadmap, starting with fundamental cases and progressively building towards more complex scenarios using established rules.
recap_md: - Start by finding the limits of basic, simple functions. - Use a set of theorems to combine these basic limits to evaluate more complex functions.

title: Theorem 1.2.1 Basic Limits
one_liner: Theorem 1.2.1 establishes the fundamental limits for a constant function, the identity function, and the one-sided limits of $1/x$ as $x$ approaches zero.
content: 1.2.1 Theorem Let $a$ and $k$ be real numbers. (a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} k=k$ (b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} x=a$ (c) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} \frac{1}{x}=-\infty$ (d) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{1}{x}=+\infty$
motivation_md: These basic limits serve as foundational building blocks, providing the simplest cases from which more complex limits can be derived using subsequent limit laws and theorems.
recap_md: - The limit of a constant $k$ as $x \rightarrow a$ is $k$. - The limit of $x$ as $x \rightarrow a$ is $a$. - The one-sided limits of $1/x$ as $x \rightarrow 0$ are $\pm\infty$.

title: Theorem 1.2.2 Properties of Limits (Limit Laws)
one_liner: Theorem 1.2.2, known as the Limit Laws, provides rules for finding limits of sums, differences, products, quotients, and roots of functions, provided individual limits exist.
content: 1.2.2 THEOREM Let $a$ be a real number, and suppose that $$\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L_{1} \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{2}$$ That is, the limits exist and have values $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$, respectively. Then: (a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)+g(x)]=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)+\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{1}+L_{2}$ (b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)-g(x)]=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)-\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{1}-L_{2}$ (c) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x) g(x)]=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)\right)\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)\right)=L_{1} L_{2}$ (d) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)}{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)}=\frac{L_{1}}{L_{2}}, \quad$ provided $L_{2} \neq 0$ (e) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \sqrt[n]{f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{L_{1}}$, provided $L_{1}>0$ if $n$ is even. Moreover, these statements are also true for the one-sided limits as $x \rightarrow a^{-}$or as $x \rightarrow a^{+}$.
motivation_md: These laws allow us to break down complex limit problems into simpler, manageable parts, making it possible to evaluate limits of algebraic combinations of functions without resorting to the formal definition every time.
recap_md: - Limits can be distributed over sums, differences, and products of functions. - The limit of a quotient is the quotient of the limits, provided the denominator's limit is not zero. - The limit of a root is the root of the limit, with conditions for even roots.

title: Constant Factor Rule for Limits
one_liner: A constant factor can be moved through a limit symbol, simplifying the evaluation of limits involving scalar multiplication.
content: A constant factor can be moved through a limit symbol.
motivation_md: This rule simplifies limit calculations by allowing constants to be factored out, reducing the complexity of the expression inside the limit and making it easier to apply other limit laws.
recap_md: - If $c$ is a constant, then $\lim_{x \rightarrow a} [c \cdot f(x)] = c \cdot \lim_{x \rightarrow a} f(x)$.

title: Theorem 1.2.3 Limit of a Polynomial
one_liner: Theorem 1.2.3 states that the limit of any polynomial function $p(x)$ as $x$ approaches a real number $a$ is simply $p(a)$.
content: 1.2.3 THEOREM For any polynomial $$\p(x)=c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}$$ and any real number $a$, $$\lim _{x \rightarrow a} p(x)=c_{0}+c_{1} a+\cdots+c_{n} a^{n}=p(a)$$
motivation_md: This theorem provides a direct and simple method for evaluating limits of polynomial functions, eliminating the need to apply individual limit laws repeatedly and streamlining calculations.
recap_md: - For a polynomial $p(x)$, the limit as $x \rightarrow a$ is found by direct substitution. - The limit value is simply $p(a)$.

title: Limits of Rational Functions with Zero Denominator and Nonzero Numerator
one_liner: When the limit of a rational function's denominator is zero but its numerator is not, the limit of the function does not exist and typically approaches $\pm\infty$.
content: The method used in the last example will not work for rational functions in which the limit of the denominator is zero because Theorem 1.2.2(d) is not applicable. There are two cases of this type to be considered: the case where the limit of the denominator is zero and the limit of the numerator is not, and the case where the limits of the numerator and denominator are both zero. If the limit of the denominator is zero but the limit of the numerator is not, then one can prove that the limit of the rational function does not exist and that one of the following situations occurs: - The limit may be $-\infty$ from one side and $+\infty$ from the other. - The limit may be $+\infty$. - The limit may be $-\infty$.
motivation_md: Understanding this case is crucial because direct substitution or simple limit laws fail when the denominator approaches zero, indicating a vertical asymptote or infinite discontinuity, which needs careful analysis.
recap_md: - If $\lim_{x \rightarrow a} q(x) = 0$ and $\lim_{x \rightarrow a} p(x) \neq 0$, then $\lim_{x \rightarrow a} p(x)/q(x)$ does not exist. - The limit will typically be $\pm\infty$ or approach different infinities from each side.

title: Computing Limits by Canceling Common Factors
one_liner: When a rational function has both numerator and denominator approaching zero, common factors of $x-a$ can be canceled to find the limit of the simplified function.
content: In the case where $p(x) / q(x)$ is a rational function for which $p(a)=0$ and $q(a)=0$, the numerator and denominator must have one or more common factors of $x-a$. In this situation, the limit of $p(x) / q(x)$ as $x \rightarrow a$ can be found by canceling all common factors of $x-a$ and then using one of the methods already considered to find the limit of the simplified function.
motivation_md: This technique addresses indeterminate forms like $0/0$, allowing us to simplify the expression and evaluate the limit, revealing the function's behavior near the point of discontinuity.
recap_md: - If $p(a)=0$ and $q(a)=0$ for a rational function $p(x)/q(x)$, both have a common factor of $(x-a)$. - Cancel these common factors to simplify the function. - Evaluate the limit of the simplified function using other methods.

title: End behavior of a function

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

one_liner: The end behavior of a function describes how its values $f(x)$ behave as the variable $x$ increases or decreases without bound (approaches $\pm\infty$).
content: If the values of a variable $x$ increase without bound, then we write $x \rightarrow+\infty$, and if the values of $x$ decrease without bound, then we write $x \rightarrow-\infty$. The behavior of a function $f(x)$ as $x$ increases without bound or decreases without bound is sometimes called the end behavior of the function. For example,
motivation_md: Understanding end behavior helps visualize the overall shape of a function's graph and predict its long-term trends, which is crucial in many applications, including modeling real-world phenomena.
recap_md: - $x \rightarrow+\infty$ means $x$ increases without bound. - $x \rightarrow-\infty$ means $x$ decreases without bound. - End behavior describes $f(x)$ as $x \rightarrow \pm\infty$.

title: Limits at Infinity (An Informal View)

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

one_liner: If the values of $f(x)$ eventually get as close as we like to a number $L$ as $x$ increases or decreases without bound, then $L$ is the limit of $f(x)$ at infinity.
content: If the values of $f(x)$ eventually get as close as desired to a number $L$ as $x$ increases without bound, then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$ or $f(x) \rightarrow L \text { as } x \rightarrow+\infty$. Similarly, if the values of $f(x)$ eventually get as close as desired to a number $L$ as $x$ decreases without bound, then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=L$ or $f(x) \rightarrow L \text { as } x \rightarrow-\infty$.
motivation_md: This concept allows us to describe the "end behavior" of a function, indicating what value the function approaches as its input grows infinitely large or infinitely small. It's crucial for understanding how functions behave over very long ranges and for identifying horizontal asymptotes.
recap_md: - A limit at positive infinity means $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ increases indefinitely.

title: Horizontal Asymptote

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

one_liner: A line $y=L$ is a horizontal asymptote for the graph of $f$ if $f(x)$ eventually comes as close as we like to $L$ as $x$ increases or decreases without bound.
content: If the graph of $f$ eventually comes as close as we like to the line $y=L$ as $x$ increases without bound, or if it eventually comes as close as we like to the line $y=L$ as $x$ decreases without bound, then we call the line $y=L$ a horizontal asymptote for the graph of $f$. This occurs if either $\lim_{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$ or $\lim_{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=L$ holds.
motivation_md: Horizontal asymptotes are important for understanding the long-term behavior of a function and for sketching its graph. They indicate a value that the function approaches as its input becomes extremely large or small, showing where the graph flattens out.
recap_md: - A horizontal asymptote $y=L$ exists if $\lim_{x \rightarrow +\infty} f(x) = L$.

title: Limit Laws for Limits at Infinity

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

one_liner: The limit laws, including those for powers and constant multiples, apply without change to limits at positive and negative infinity.
content: The limit laws from Theorem 1.2.2 carry over without change to limits at $+\infty$ and $-\infty$. Additionally, if $n$ is a positive integer, it follows that $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}(f(x))^{n}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)\right)^{n}$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}(f(x))^{n}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)\right)^{n}$, provided the indicated limit of $f(x)$ exists. Constants can also be moved through the limit symbols for limits at infinity: $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} k f(x)=k \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} k f(x)=k \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)$, provided the indicated limit of $f(x)$ exists. Finally, if $f(x)=k$ is a constant function, its values do not change as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, so $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} k=k$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} k=k$.
motivation_md: These laws simplify the computation of limits at infinity for complex functions by allowing us to break them down into simpler, known limits. They provide a systematic way to evaluate limits of sums, products, quotients, and powers of functions as $x$ approaches infinity.
recap_md: - Standard limit laws apply to limits as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$.

title: Infinite Limits at Infinity (An Informal View)

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

one_liner: If the values of $f(x)$ increase or decrease without bound as $x$ approaches positive or negative infinity, this is an infinite limit at infinity.
content: If the values of $f(x)$ increase without bound as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=+\infty$ or $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=+\infty$, as appropriate. Similarly, if the values of $f(x)$ decrease without bound as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=-\infty$ or $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=-\infty$, as appropriate.
motivation_md: This concept describes functions whose values grow or shrink indefinitely as $x$ moves far from the origin, helping to characterize their unbounded end behavior. It's essential for understanding functions that do not approach a finite horizontal asymptote.
recap_md: - If $f(x)$ increases without bound as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$, we write $\lim_{x \rightarrow \pm \infty} f(x) = +\infty$.

title: Limits of $x^n$ as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

one_liner: For positive integers $n$, $\lim_{x \rightarrow+\infty} x^{n}=+\infty$, while $\lim_{x \rightarrow-\infty} x^{n}$ is $\pm\infty$ depending on whether $n$ is even or odd.
content: Figure 1.3.5 illustrates the end behavior of the polynomials $x^{n}$ for $n=1,2,3$, and 4. These are special cases of the following general results: $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} x^{n}=+\infty$ for $n=1,2,3, \ldots$. For $x \rightarrow-\infty$, the limit is $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} x^{n}= \begin{cases}-\infty, & n=1,3,5, \ldots \\ +\infty, & n=2,4,6, \ldots\end{cases}$.
motivation_md: Understanding the end behavior of simple power functions $x^n$ is fundamental because these are the building blocks for polynomials. This theorem allows us to predict the long-term trends of these basic functions, which is crucial for analyzing more complex expressions.
recap_md: - For any positive integer $n$, $\lim_{x \rightarrow +\infty} x^n = +\infty$.

title: Limits of Polynomials as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

one_liner: The end behavior of a polynomial as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$ matches the end behavior of its highest degree term.
content: There is a useful principle about polynomials which, expressed informally, states: The end behavior of a polynomial matches the end behavior of its highest degree term. More precisely, if $c_{n} \neq 0$, then $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}\left(c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}\right) =\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} c_{n} x^{n}$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}\right) =\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} c_{n} x^{n}$. We can motivate these results by factoring out the highest power of $x$ from the polynomial and examining the limit of the factored expression: $c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}=x^{n}\left(\frac{c_{0}}{x^{n}}+\frac{c_{1}}{x^{n-1}}+\cdots+c_{n}\right)$. As $x \rightarrow-\infty$ or $x \rightarrow+\infty$, all terms with positive powers of $x$ in the denominator approach 0, making these results plausible.
motivation_md: This theorem provides a powerful shortcut for determining the end behavior of any polynomial, simplifying what could otherwise be complex limit calculations by focusing only on the dominant term. It's a fundamental principle for analyzing polynomial functions.
recap_md: - The end behavior of a polynomial matches its highest degree term.

title: Computing Limits of Rational Functions by Dividing by Highest Power

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

one_liner: One technique for determining the end behavior of a rational function is to divide each term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ that occurs in the denominator.
content: One technique for determining the end behavior of a rational function is to divide each term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ that occurs in the denominator. After this division, the limiting behavior can be determined using results that have already been established. This method is illustrated with examples.
motivation_md: This technique transforms complex rational functions into a form where individual term limits can be easily evaluated, allowing for a systematic approach to finding limits at infinity. It simplifies the expression to reveal its dominant behavior.
recap_md: - Divide all terms in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator.

title: Quick Method for Finding Limits of Rational Functions as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$

position.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

one_liner: The end behavior of a rational function matches the end behavior of the quotient of the highest degree term in the numerator divided by the highest degree term in the denominator.
content: The end behavior of a rational function matches the end behavior of the quotient of the highest degree term in the numerator divided by the highest degree term in the denominator.
motivation_md: This quick method provides an efficient way to determine the end behavior of rational functions without extensive algebraic manipulation, making limit calculations faster for common cases. It leverages the principle of dominant terms at infinity.
recap_md: - Identify the highest degree term in the numerator.

title: Differentiating a Power Function
one_liner: To differentiate a power function, decrease the constant exponent by one and multiply the resulting power function by the original exponent.
content: To differentiate a power function, decrease the constant exponent by one and multiply the resulting power function by the original exponent.
motivation_md: This technique provides a straightforward and efficient method for finding the derivative of power functions, avoiding the more complex limit definition of the derivative.
recap_md: - Decrease the exponent by one. - Multiply the function by the original exponent.

title: Derivative of a Constant Times a Function
one_liner: The derivative of a constant times a function, $(c f)^{\prime}$, is equal to the constant times the derivative of the function, $c f^{\prime}$.
content: The derivative of a constant times a function can be expressed in function notation as $$(c f)^{\prime}=c f^{\prime}$$ This is also known as Formula (8).
motivation_md: This formula simplifies the process of differentiating functions that are scaled by a constant, allowing the constant to be factored out before differentiation.
recap_md: - The derivative of $c f(x)$ is $c f'(x)$. - A constant factor can be moved outside the derivative operation.

title: Theorem 2.3.4: Constant Multiple Rule
one_liner: The Constant Multiple Rule states that if a function $f$ is differentiable at $x$ and $c$ is any real number, then $c f$ is also differentiable at $x$, and its derivative is $c$ times the derivative of $f$.
content: Theorem 2.3.4, known as the Constant Multiple Rule, states that if a function $f$ is differentiable at $x$ and $c$ is any real number, then the function $c f$ is also differentiable at $x$. The derivative is given by the formula: $$\frac{d}{d x}[c f(x)]=c \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)] \tag{8}$$ The proof proceeds from the limit definition of the derivative: $$\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{d x}[c f(x)] & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{c f(x+h)-c f(x)}{h} \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} c\left[\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\right] \\ & =c \lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \quad \text { A constant factor can be } \\ & =c \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]\end{aligned}$$ This demonstrates that a constant factor can be moved through a limit sign.
motivation_md: This theorem is a fundamental property of derivatives, establishing that scaling a function by a constant simply scales its derivative by the same constant. It simplifies differentiation by allowing constants to be factored out.
recap_md: - If $f$ is differentiable, then $c f$ is also differentiable. - The derivative of $c f(x)$ is $c$ times the derivative of $f(x)$.

title: Moving a Constant Factor Through a Derivative Sign
one_liner: A constant factor can be moved through a derivative sign, simplifying the differentiation process.
content: In words, a constant factor can be moved through a derivative sign.
motivation_md: This technique simplifies the process of finding derivatives by allowing us to factor out constants, making the remaining differentiation task easier to manage.
recap_md: - Constants can be pulled out of a derivative operation. - This is an application of the Constant Multiple Rule.

title: Theorem 2.3.5: Sum and Difference Rules
one_liner: The Sum and Difference Rules state that if functions $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $x$, then the derivative of their sum is the sum of their derivatives, and the derivative of their difference is the difference of their derivatives.
content: Theorem 2.3.5, known as the Sum and Difference Rules, states that if functions $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $x$, then their sum $f+g$ and their difference $f-g$ are also differentiable at $x$. The formulas are: $$\begin{align*}& \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)+g(x)]=\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]+\frac{d}{d x}[g(x)] \tag{9}\\& \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)-g(x)]=\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]-\frac{d}{d x}[g(x)] \tag{10}\end{align*}$$ Formula (9) can be proved as follows: $$\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)+g(x)] & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{[f(x+h)+g(x+h)]-[f(x)+g(x)]}{h} \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{[f(x+h)-f(x)]+[g(x+h)-g(x)]}{h} \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}+\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{g(x+h)-g(x)}{h} \quad \text { The limit of a sum is } \\ & =\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]+\frac{d}{d x}[g(x)]\end{aligned}$$ Formula (10) can be proved similarly, or by writing $f(x)-g(x)$ as $f(x)+(-1) g(x)$ and applying Formulas (8) and (9).
motivation_md: These rules are crucial for differentiating complex functions by breaking them down into simpler sums or differences of functions. They allow us to apply differentiation rules to each component separately.
recap_md: - The derivative of a sum of functions is the sum of their derivatives. - The derivative of a difference of functions is the difference of their derivatives.

title: Differentiating Sums and Differences
one_liner: The derivative of a sum equals the sum of the derivatives, and the derivative of a difference equals the difference of the derivatives.
content: In words, the derivative of a sum equals the sum of the derivatives, and the derivative of a difference equals the difference of the derivatives.
motivation_md: This technique allows us to differentiate functions that are formed by adding or subtracting simpler functions, making the process more manageable than using the limit definition directly.
recap_md: - To differentiate a sum, differentiate each term and add the results. - To differentiate a difference, differentiate each term and subtract the results.

title: Higher Derivatives
one_liner: The derivative of a function is itself a function, which can be differentiated again to obtain second, third, and even higher derivatives.
content: The derivative $f^{\prime}$ of a function $f$ is itself a function and hence may have a derivative of its own. If $f^{\prime}$ is differentiable, then its derivative is denoted by $f^{\prime \prime}$ and is called the second derivative of $f$. As long as differentiability holds, the process of differentiating can continue to obtain third, fourth, fifth, and even higher derivatives of $f$. These successive derivatives are denoted by various notations.
motivation_md: Higher derivatives provide deeper insights into a function's behavior beyond its immediate rate of change. For instance, the second derivative reveals information about concavity and acceleration, which is crucial in physics and optimization.
recap_md: - The derivative of a function $f^{\prime}$ can also be differentiated. - The derivative of $f^{\prime}$ is called the second derivative, denoted $f^{\prime \prime}$. - This process can continue to find third, fourth, and higher derivatives.

title: Higher Order Derivatives
one_liner: Higher-order derivatives are obtained by repeatedly differentiating a function, with $f^{\prime \prime}$ being the second derivative, $f^{\prime \prime \prime}$ the third, and so on, using specific notations.
content: The derivative $f^{\prime}$ of a function $f$ is itself a function and hence may have a derivative of its own. If $f^{\prime}$ is differentiable, then its derivative is denoted by $f^{\prime \prime}$ and is called the second derivative of $f$. As long as we have differentiability, we can continue the process of differentiating to obtain third, fourth, fifth, and even higher derivatives of $f$. These successive derivatives are denoted by $$f^{\prime}, \quad f^{\prime \prime}=\left(f^{\prime}\right)^{\prime}, \quad f^{\prime \prime \prime}=\left(f^{\prime \prime}\right)^{\prime}, \quad f^{(4)}=\left(f^{\prime \prime \prime}\right)^{\prime}, \quad f^{(5)}=\left(f^{(4)}\right)^{\prime}, \ldots$$
motivation_md: Higher-order derivatives are essential for analyzing more complex aspects of a function's behavior, such as concavity, inflection points, and acceleration. They are widely used in physics, engineering, and optimization problems.
recap_md: - Higher derivatives are found by differentiating a function multiple times. - The second derivative is $f^{\prime \prime}$, the third is $f^{\prime \prime \prime}$, and subsequent derivatives use superscript numbers like $f^{(4)}$.

title: Introduction to Intermediate-Value Theorem
one_liner: If a function is continuous on a closed interval, it must take on every value between its endpoints' function values at least once.
content: Figure 1.5.8 illustrates the graph of a function that is continuous on the closed interval $[a, b]$. This figure suggests that if any horizontal line $y=k$ is drawn, where $k$ is between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then that line will intersect the curve $y=f(x)$ at least once over the interval $[a, b]$. Stated numerically, if $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, then the function $f$ must assume every value $k$ between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ at least once as $x$ varies from $a$ to $b$. For instance, the polynomial $p(x)=x^{5}-x+3$ has a value of 3 at $x=1$ and 33 at $x=2$. Due to the continuity of $p$, it follows that the equation $x^{5}-x+3=k$ has at least one solution in the interval $[1,2]$ for every value of $k$ between 3 and 33. This principle is formally stated in the subsequent theorem.
motivation_md: The Intermediate-Value Theorem provides a powerful guarantee: if a function is continuous, it cannot 'skip' any values between two points. This intuitive idea is fundamental for understanding function behavior and forms the basis for proving the existence of solutions to equations.
recap_md: - A continuous function on a closed interval $[a, b]$ must take on all values between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.- This means for any $k$ between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, there's an $x$ in $[a, b]$ such that $f(x)=k$.- The theorem ensures the existence of such values, even if we can't find them explicitly.

title: Intermediate-Value Theorem
one_liner: If $f$ is continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$ and $k$ is any number between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, inclusive, then there is at least one number $x$ in the interval $[a, b]$ such that $f(x)=k$.
content: If $f$ is continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$ and $k$ is any number between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, inclusive, then there is at least one number $x$ in the interval $[a, b]$ such that $f(x)=k$.
motivation_md: This theorem formalizes the intuitive idea that a continuous function cannot 'jump over' any value between its endpoints. It's crucial for proving the existence of solutions to equations and underpins many numerical methods.
recap_md: - Requires $f$ to be continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$.- Guarantees that $f(x)=k$ for any $k$ between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.- Ensures the existence of at least one $x$ in $[a, b]$ for which this holds.

title: Approximating roots using the Intermediate-Value Theorem
one_liner: Many problems require finding roots of $f(x)=0$, and when exact algebraic solutions are not possible, the Intermediate-Value Theorem provides a method for approximating these roots.
content: [FIGURE:5ea34ea08d81bc20 | A graph on an $xy$-plane displays a continuous function $y = f(x)$. At $x=a$, the function value $f(a)$ is positive, and at $x=b$, the function value $f(b)$ is negative. The curve connects these...] △ Figure 1.5.9 (see figure: The graph shows the curve of the function $y = x^3 - x - 1$ on a Cartesian coordinate system. The continuous curve passes through the y-axis at $(0, -1)$, exhibits a local maximum for negative $x$...) $ Figure 1.5.10 A variety of problems can be reduced to solving an equation $f(x)=0$ for its roots. While it is sometimes possible to solve for roots exactly using algebra, this is often not feasible, requiring one to settle for decimal approximations. One procedure for approximating roots is based on a specific consequence of the Intermediate-Value Theorem.
motivation_md: Not all equations can be solved algebraically for exact roots. This technique provides a systematic way to find numerical approximations, which is essential for practical applications where exact solutions are either impossible or unnecessary.
recap_md: - Addresses problems requiring solutions to $f(x)=0$ (finding roots).- Used when exact algebraic solutions are not possible.- Relies on a specific consequence of the Intermediate-Value Theorem for approximation.

title: Existence of a root (IVT consequence)
one_liner: If a continuous function $f$ on $[a, b]$ has $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ with opposite signs, then there is at least one root $f(x)=0$ in $(a, b)$.
content: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, and if $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ are nonzero and have opposite signs, then there is at least one solution of the equation $f(x)=0$ in the interval ( $a, b$ ).
motivation_md: This theorem is a direct application of the Intermediate-Value Theorem, specifically tailored to guarantee the existence of a root (where $f(x)=0$). It forms the theoretical basis for numerical root-finding methods like the bisection method.
recap_md: - Requires $f$ to be continuous on $[a, b]$.- Requires $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ to be non-zero and have opposite signs.- Guarantees at least one root $x$ such that $f(x)=0$ exists in $(a, b)$.

title: Absolute error
one_liner: The absolute error in an approximation $x$ to a quantity $x_0$ is defined as the absolute difference between them, $\epsilon = |x - x_0|$.
content: Before illustrating how the theorem can be used to approximate roots, it is helpful to discuss standard terminology for describing errors in approximations. If $x$ is an approximation to a quantity $x_{0}$, then we define $$ \epsilon=\left|x-x_{0}\right| $$ as the absolute error or, less precisely, simply the error in the approximation. The terminology in Table 1.5.1 is used to describe the size of such errors.
motivation_md: When using approximations, it's crucial to quantify how accurate they are. Absolute error provides a fundamental measure of the difference between an approximate value and the true value, allowing for precise communication of accuracy.
recap_md: - If $x$ approximates $x_0$, the absolute error is $\epsilon = |x - x_0|$.- This value quantifies the magnitude of the difference between the approximation and the true value.- It is also sometimes referred to simply as the 'error'.

title: Approximating roots using technology
one_liner: A graphing or calculating utility can approximate a root $x_0$ to a specified decimal-place accuracy, such as $x_0 \approx 1.3245$ to three decimal places.
content: Use a graphing or calculating utility to show that the root $x_{0}$ in Example 5 can be approximated as $x_{0} \approx 1.3245$ to three decimal-place accuracy.
motivation_md: While theoretical methods like the IVT guarantee root existence, practical applications often require numerical values. Technology provides efficient ways to quickly find highly accurate approximations of roots, saving time and effort.
recap_md: - Utilizes graphing or calculating utilities for root approximation.- Aims to achieve a specific decimal-place accuracy.- For example, approximating $x_0 \approx 1.3245$ to three decimal places.

title: Understanding decimal place accuracy
one_liner: Approximating a number to $n$ decimal places means the absolute error is less than $0.5 \times 10^{-n}$, which does not guarantee the first $n$ rounded decimal places will match.
content: To state that $x$ approximates $x_{0}$ to $n$ decimal places does not imply that the first $n$ decimal places of $x$ and $x_{0}$ will be identical when the numbers are rounded to $n$ decimal places. For example, $x=1.084$ approximates $x_{0}=1.087$ to two decimal places because the absolute difference, $\left|x-x_{0}\right|=0.003$, is less than 0.005. However, if we round these values to two decimal places, we get $x \approx 1.08$ and $x_{0} \approx 1.09$. Therefore, when approximating a number to $n$ decimal places, you should display that approximation to at least $n+1$ decimal places to ensure the accuracy is preserved.
motivation_md: Understanding decimal place accuracy is crucial for correctly interpreting and reporting numerical approximations. This concept clarifies a common misconception, ensuring that accuracy is preserved and communicated effectively in scientific and mathematical contexts.
recap_md: - Approximating to $n$ decimal places means $|x-x_0| < 0.5 \times 10^{-n}$.- This condition does not guarantee that the first $n$ rounded decimal places of $x$ and $x_0$ will be the same.- To preserve accuracy, an approximation to $n$ decimal places should be displayed with at least $n+1$ decimal places.

title: Continuity of Sine and Cosine Functions

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

one_liner: The sine and cosine functions are continuous everywhere, as their graphs are continuous curves and their limits as $x$ approaches $c$ equal $\sin c$ and $\cos c$ respectively.
content: Recall from trigonometry that the graphs of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are drawn as continuous curves. While a formal proof of their continuity will not be provided here, we can motivate this fact by considering a fixed angle $c$ in radian measure and a variable angle $x$ also in radian measure. As illustrated in Figure 1.6.1, if the angle $x$ approaches the angle $c$, then the point $P(\cos x, \sin x)$ moves along the unit circle toward $Q(\cos c, \sin c)$. Consequently, the coordinates of $P$ approach the corresponding coordinates of $Q$. This implies that $$ \begin{equation*} \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \sin x=\sin c \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \cos x=\cos c \tag{1} \end{equation*} $$ Thus, $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are continuous at any arbitrary point $c$, meaning these functions are continuous everywhere.
motivation_md: Understanding the continuity of trigonometric functions like sine and cosine is fundamental for calculus. It allows us to apply theorems (like the Intermediate-Value Theorem) and techniques (like differentiation) that rely on continuous behavior, simplifying many mathematical analyses.
recap_md: - The graphs of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are continuous curves.- As $x$ approaches $c$, the point $(\cos x, \sin x)$ on the unit circle approaches $(\cos c, \sin c)$.- This geometric intuition shows that $\lim_{x \to c} \sin x = \sin c$ and $\lim_{x \to c} \cos x = \cos c$, confirming continuity everywhere.

title: Alternative formulas for rates of change

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

one_liner: Average and instantaneous rates of change can be expressed using an alternative formula where $h = x_1 - x_0$.
content: If desired, the formulas for average and instantaneous rates of change can be rewritten by letting $h=x_{1}-x_{0}$. The average rate of change, $r_{\mathrm{ave}}$, is then given by:$$r_{\mathrm{ave}}=\frac{f\left(x_{0}+h\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{h}  \tag{10}$$And the instantaneous rate of change, $r_{\mathrm{inst}}$, is given by:$$r_{\mathrm{inst}}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\left(x_{0}+h\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{h} \tag{11}$$
motivation_md: These alternative formulas simplify the notation for calculating rates of change, especially when working with limits. By introducing $h$ as the difference between two $x$-values, the expressions become more concise and easier to manipulate in calculus.
recap_md: - The average rate of change can be written as $r_{\mathrm{ave}}=\frac{f\left(x_{0}+h\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{h}$.

title: Rates of Change in Applications and Units

position.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

one_liner: In applied problems, units for a rate of change are found by dividing the units of the dependent variable by the units of the independent variable.
content: In applied problems, both average and instantaneous rates of change must be accompanied by appropriate units. Generally, the units for a rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ are obtained by "dividing" the units of $y$ by the units of $x$, then simplifying according to standard algebraic rules. For example:If $y$ is in degrees Fahrenheit ( ${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$ ) and $x$ is in inches (in), then a rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ has units of degrees Fahrenheit per inch ( ${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{F} / \mathrm{in}$ ).If $y$ is in feet per second ( $\mathrm{ft} / \mathrm{s}$ ) and $x$ is in seconds (s), then a rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ has units of feet per second per second ( $\mathrm{ft} / \mathrm{s} / \mathrm{s}$ ), which is usually written as $\mathrm{ft} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$.If $y$ is in newton-meters $(\mathrm{N} \cdot \mathrm{m})$ and $x$ is in meters $(\mathrm{m})$, then a rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ has units of newtons ( N ), since $\mathrm{N} \cdot \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{m}=\mathrm{N}$.If $y$ is in foot-pounds ( $\mathrm{ft} \cdot \mathrm{lb}$ ) and $x$ is in hours (h), then a rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ has units of foot-pounds per hour ( $\mathrm{ft} \cdot \mathrm{lb} / \mathrm{h}$ ).
motivation_md: Understanding how to determine and simplify units for rates of change is crucial for interpreting results in real-world applications. Correct units ensure that the calculated rates have physical meaning and can be accurately communicated in scientific and engineering contexts.
recap_md: - Units for rates of change are derived by dividing the units of the output variable by the units of the input variable.

title: The Derivative Function
aliases: derivative of f with respect to x
one_liner: The derivative function $f^{\prime}$ is defined by the limit $f^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$, where the limit exists.
content: The function $f^{\prime}$ defined by the formula:$$f^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \tag{2}$$is called the derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$. The domain of $f^{\prime}$ consists of all $x$ in the domain of $f$ for which this limit exists.
motivation_md: This definition formalizes the concept of instantaneous rate of change and the slope of a tangent line. It provides a fundamental tool for analyzing how functions change, enabling the study of motion, optimization, and many other dynamic processes in mathematics and science.
recap_md: - The derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is denoted $f^{\prime}(x)$.

title: Finding an Equation for the Tangent Line to y=f(x) at x=x0
one_liner: To find the equation of a tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $x=x_0$, evaluate $f(x_0)$, find $f'(x_0)$ for the slope, then use the point-slope form.
content: To find an equation for the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $x=x_{0}$, follow these steps:Step 1. Evaluate $f\left(x_{0}\right)$; the point of tangency is $\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$.Step 2. Find $f^{\prime}(x)$ and evaluate $f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)$, which is the slope $m$ of the line.Step 3. Substitute the value of the slope $m$ and the point $\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ into the point-slope form of the line:$$y-f\left(x_{0}\right)=f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)\left(x-x_{0}\right)$$or, equivalently:$$y=f\left(x_{0}\right)+f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)\left(x-x_{0}\right) \tag{3}$$
motivation_md: This technique allows us to find the equation of the line that best approximates a function's behavior at a specific point. This is crucial for local approximations, understanding instantaneous rates of change, and solving optimization problems.
recap_md: - Find the point of tangency $(x_0, f(x_0))$.

title: Differentiable at a Point
one_liner: A function $f$ is differentiable at $x_0$ if the limit defining $f^{\prime}(x_0)$ exists, and differentiable on an interval if it is differentiable at every point within it.
content: A function $f$ is said to be differentiable at $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{0}}$ if the limit:$$f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\left(x_{0}+h\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{h} \tag{5}$$exists. If $f$ is differentiable at each point of an open interval $(a, b)$, then we say that it is differentiable on $(\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b})$. Similarly, this applies to open intervals of the form $(a,+\infty)$, $(-\infty, b)$, and $(-\infty,+\infty)$. In the last case, we say that $f$ is differentiable everywhere.
motivation_md: Differentiability is a key property indicating that a function is "smooth" enough to have a well-defined tangent line at a point. This is essential for applying calculus techniques like optimization, related rates, and understanding the local behavior of functions.
recap_md: - A function $f$ is differentiable at $x_0$ if $f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\left(x_{0}+h\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{h}$ exists.

title: Geometric Interpretation of Differentiability and Non-Differentiability
one_liner: Geometrically, a function is differentiable at $x_0$ if its graph has a unique nonvertical tangent line at that point, failing at corners or vertical tangents.
content: Geometrically, a function $f$ is differentiable at $x_{0}$ if the graph of $f$ has a tangent line at $x_{0}$. Conversely, $f$ is not differentiable at any point $x_{0}$ where the secant lines from $P\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ to points $Q(x, f(x))$ distinct from $P$ do not approach a unique nonvertical limiting position as $x \rightarrow x_{0}$. Figure 2.2.6 illustrates two common ways in which a function that is continuous at $x_{0}$ can fail to be differentiable at $x_{0}$. These can be described informally as corner points and points of vertical tangency.At a corner point, the slopes of the secant lines have different limits from the left and from the right, meaning the two-sided limit that defines the derivative does not exist (Figure 2.2.7). At a point of vertical tangency, the slopes of the secant lines approach $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ from the left and from the right (Figure 2.2.8), so again the limit that defines the derivative does not exist.
motivation_md: Understanding the geometric interpretation helps visualize differentiability and quickly identify points where a derivative might not exist. This intuition complements the analytical definition, making it easier to grasp the concept of "smoothness" in a function's graph.
recap_md: - Differentiability at $x_0$ means the graph has a tangent line at $x_0$.

title: Differentiability and Magnification
one_liner: Differentiability at a point means that under strong magnification, the graph of the function at that point appears as a nonvertical straight line.
content: [FIGURE:a61c122aca4e7637 | A graph shows a blue curve in a coordinate system, descending steeply from left to right. A point $P$ is marked on the curve, corresponding to $x_0$ on the x-axis. Several other points, collectively...]Differentiability at $x_{0}$ can also be described informally in terms of the behavior of the graph of $f$ under increasingly stronger magnification at the point $P\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ (Figure 2.2.9). If $f$ is differentiable at $x_{0}$, then under sufficiently strong magnification at $P$ the graph looks like a nonvertical line (the tangent line). If a corner point occurs at $x_{0}$, then no matter how great the magnification at $P$ the corner persists and the graph never looks like a nonvertical line. If vertical tangency occurs at $x_{0}$, then the graph of $f$ looks like a vertical line under sufficiently strong magnification at $P$.
motivation_md: This informal description provides an intuitive way to understand differentiability, allowing one to visualize the "smoothness" required for a derivative to exist. It helps build a conceptual bridge between the analytical definition and the visual representation of a function.
recap_md: - If $f$ is differentiable at $x_0$, its graph looks like a nonvertical line under strong magnification at $P(x_0, f(x_0))$.

title: Contrapositive Form of a Theorem
one_liner: The contrapositive form of 'If A is true, then B is true' is 'If B is not true, then A is not true', and these two statements are logically equivalent.
content: A theorem that says "If statement $A$ is true, then statement $B$ is true" is equivalent to the theorem that says "If statement $B$ is not true, then statement $A$ is not true." The two theorems are called contrapositive forms of one another. For example, Theorem 2.2.3 can be rewritten in contrapositive form as "If a function $f$ is not continuous at $x_{0}$, then $f$ is not differentiable at $x_{0} .^{\prime\prime}$
motivation_md: Understanding contrapositive statements is crucial for logical reasoning in mathematics, allowing for alternative ways to prove theorems or understand their implications. It's a powerful tool for constructing proofs and analyzing the logical structure of mathematical statements.
recap_md: - A theorem "If A, then B" is logically equivalent to its contrapositive.

title: Limits as x approaches +/- Infinity (Intuitive)
one_liner: The limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$ means $f(x)$ gets arbitrarily close to $L$ as $x$ becomes sufficiently large, and similarly for $x \rightarrow-\infty$.
content: In Section 1.3, we discussed the limits $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=L$ from an intuitive perspective. The first limit means that we can make the value of $f(x)$ as close as we like to $L$ by taking $x$ sufficiently large. The second limit means that we can make the value of $f(x)$ as close as we like to $L$ by taking $x$ sufficiently far to the left of 0. These ideas are formally captured in subsequent definitions and are illustrated in Figure 1.4.4.
motivation_md: These limits describe the behavior of a function as its input grows infinitely large or infinitely small, allowing us to understand end behavior without needing to evaluate the function at extreme values.
recap_md: - $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$ means $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ gets very large. - $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=L$ means $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ gets very far to the left of 0.

title: Limit as x approaches +Infinity
one_liner: The limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$ means that for any $\epsilon>0$, there is an $N$ such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ whenever $x>N$.
content: Let $f(x)$ be defined for all $x$ in some infinite open interval extending in the positive $x$-direction. We will write $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$ if given any number $\epsilon>0$, there corresponds a positive number $N$ such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ if $x>N$.
motivation_md: This definition provides a rigorous way to define the end behavior of a function, ensuring that $f(x)$ can be made arbitrarily close to $L$ by taking $x$ large enough, which is crucial for formal proofs and advanced analysis.
recap_md: - $f(x)$ must be defined for all $x$ in some infinite open interval extending in the positive $x$-direction. - For any $\epsilon>0$, there exists a positive number $N$ such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ when $x>N$.

title: Limit as x approaches -Infinity
one_liner: The limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=L$ means that for any $\epsilon>0$, there is a negative $N$ such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ whenever $x<N$.
content: Let $f(x)$ be defined for all $x$ in some infinite open interval extending in the negative $x$-direction. We will write $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=L$ if given any number $\epsilon>0$, there corresponds a negative number $N$ such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ if $x<N$.
motivation_md: This definition formally describes how a function's output approaches a specific value as its input decreases without bound, providing a precise tool for analyzing the left-hand end behavior of functions.
recap_md: - $f(x)$ must be defined for all $x$ in some infinite open interval extending in the negative $x$-direction. - For any $\epsilon>0$, there exists a negative number $N$ such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ when $x<N$.

title: Infinite Limits (Intuitive)
one_liner: Infinite limits describe cases where a limit fails to exist because $f(x)$ increases or decreases without bound as $x$ approaches a specific value $a$.
content: In Section 1.1, we discussed limits of the following types from an intuitive viewpoint: $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=+\infty$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=-\infty$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=-\infty$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=+\infty$, and $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=-\infty$. Each of these expressions describes a particular way in which the limit fails to exist. The $+\infty$ indicates that the limit fails to exist because $f(x)$ increases without bound, and the $-\infty$ indicates that the limit fails to exist because $f(x)$ decreases without bound. These ideas are captured more precisely in the following definitions and are illustrated in Figure 1.4.5.
motivation_md: Understanding infinite limits allows us to characterize the behavior of functions that grow or shrink without bound near a specific point, often indicating the presence of vertical asymptotes and providing insight into function singularities.
recap_md: - Infinite limits occur when $f(x)$ increases or decreases without bound. - $+\infty$ indicates $f(x)$ increases without bound, while $-\infty$ indicates $f(x)$ decreases without bound. - These expressions describe specific ways a limit fails to exist.

title: Infinite Limit as x approaches a (to +Infinity)
one_liner: The limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=+\infty$ means that for any positive $M$, there is a $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)>M$ whenever $0<|x-a|<\delta$.
content: Let $f(x)$ be defined for all $x$ in some open interval containing $a$, except that $f(x)$ need not be defined at $a$. We will write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=+\infty$ if given any positive number $M$, we can find a number $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)$ satisfies $f(x)>M$ if $0<|x-a|<\delta$.
motivation_md: This formal definition allows us to rigorously prove that a function's output can be made arbitrarily large by keeping its input sufficiently close to $a$, which is essential for understanding vertical asymptotes and function behavior near singularities.
recap_md: - $f(x)$ must be defined in an open interval containing $a$, except possibly at $a$ itself. - For any positive $M$, there exists a $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)>M$ when $0<|x-a|<\delta$.

title: Infinite Limit as x approaches a (to -Infinity)
one_liner: The limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=-\infty$ means that for any negative $M$, there is a $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)<M$ whenever $0<|x-a|<\delta$.
content: Let $f(x)$ be defined for all $x$ in some open interval containing $a$, except that $f(x)$ need not be defined at $a$. We will write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=-\infty$ if given any negative number $M$, we can find a number $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)$ satisfies $f(x)<M$ if $0<|x-a|<\delta$.
motivation_md: This definition provides a formal way to describe how a function's output can be made arbitrarily small (large negative) by keeping its input sufficiently close to $a$, which is crucial for analyzing vertical asymptotes where a function dives downwards.
recap_md: - $f(x)$ must be defined in an open interval containing $a$, except possibly at $a$ itself. - For any negative $M$, there exists a $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)<M$ when $0<|x-a|<\delta$.

title: Introduction to Continuity
one_liner: Continuity translates the intuitive idea of an 'unbroken curve' into a precise mathematical formulation, like the trajectory of a baseball.
content: [FIGURE:08058e9f1dd66e94 | A hand is reaching upwards towards a baseball suspended in mid-air against a cloudy blue sky. This image likely serves as a decorative or introductory visual, as its direct relevance to the...] Joseph Helfenberger/iStockphoto A thrown baseball cannot vanish at some point and reappear someplace else to continue its motion. Thus, we perceive the path of the ball as an unbroken curve. In this section, we translate "unbroken curve" into a precise mathematical formulation called continuity.
motivation_md: The concept of continuity is fundamental in calculus, allowing us to describe functions whose graphs have no breaks, jumps, or holes. This property is essential for many theorems and applications, such as the Intermediate Value Theorem.
recap_md: - Continuity mathematically defines an 'unbroken curve'. - It describes functions whose graphs have no sudden jumps or gaps. - The path of a thrown baseball is an intuitive example of continuous motion.

title: Conditions for discontinuity
one_liner: A function has a discontinuity at $x=c$ if it is undefined at $c$, its limit does not exist at $c$, or its function value and limit at $c$ are different.
content: Intuitively, the graph of a function can be described as a "continuous curve" if it has no breaks or holes. To make this idea more precise, we need to understand what properties of a function can cause breaks or holes. Referring to Figure 1.5.1, we see that the graph of a function has a break or hole if any of the following conditions occur: - The function $f$ is undefined at $c$ (Figure 1.5.1a). - The limit of $f(x)$ does not exist as $x$ approaches $c$ (Figures 1.5.1b, 1.5.1c). - The value of the function and the value of the limit at $c$ are different (Figure 1.5.1d). If one or more of these conditions fails to hold, then we say that $f$ has a discontinuity at $x=c$. Each function drawn in Figure 1.5.1 illustrates a discontinuity at $x=c$. In Figure 1.5.1a, the function is not defined at $c$, violating the first condition of Definition 1.5.1. In Figure 1.5.1b, the one-sided limits of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $c$ both exist but are not equal, so $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ does not exist, violating the second condition of Definition 1.5.1. A function like this has a jump discontinuity at $c$. In Figure 1.5.1c, the one-sided limits of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $c$ are infinite, so $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ does not exist, violating the second condition of Definition 1.5.1. A function like this has an infinite discontinuity at $c$. In Figure 1.5.1d, the function is defined at $c$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ exists, but these two values are not equal, violating the third condition of Definition 1.5.1. A function like this has a removable discontinuity at $c$. Exercises 33 and 34 help to explain why discontinuities of this type are given this name.
motivation_md: Identifying the conditions for discontinuity helps us understand precisely where and why a function's graph might have breaks or holes. This clarity is vital for analyzing function behavior, ensuring mathematical rigor, and applying theorems that rely on continuity.
recap_md: - A discontinuity occurs if $f(c)$ is undefined, $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ does not exist, or $f(c) \neq \lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$. - Jump discontinuities happen when one-sided limits exist but are unequal. - Infinite discontinuities occur when one-sided limits are infinite. - Removable discontinuities occur when the limit exists but doesn't match $f(c)$ or $f(c)$ is undefined.

title: Theorem 1.6.1: Continuity of Trigonometric Functions

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

one_liner: If $c$ is any number in the natural domain of a trigonometric function, then the limit of the function as $x$ approaches $c$ is equal to the function evaluated at $c$.
content: If $c$ is any number in the natural domain of the stated trigonometric function, then the limit of the function as $x$ approaches $c$ is equal to the function evaluated at $c$. This means that all six trigonometric functions are continuous on their natural domains:$$ \begin{array}{lll} \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \sin x=\sin c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \cos x=\cos c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \tan x=\tan c \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \csc x=\csc c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \sec x=\sec c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \cot x=\cot c \end{array} $$
motivation_md: This theorem formally establishes that trigonometric functions are continuous wherever they are defined. This property is crucial because it allows for direct substitution to evaluate limits of trigonometric expressions, simplifying calculations and enabling further analysis in calculus.
recap_md: - Trigonometric functions are continuous on their natural domains.- For any trigonometric function $f(x)$, if $c$ is in its domain, then $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$.

title: Continuity of Inverse Functions

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

one_liner: Geometrically, if a one-to-one function has no breaks or holes, its inverse also has no breaks, suggesting that the inverse of a continuous function is continuous.
content: Since the graphs of a one-to-one function $f$ and its inverse $f^{-1}$ are reflections of one another about the line $y=x$, it is geometrically clear that if the graph of $f$ has no breaks or holes in it, then neither does the graph of $f^{-1}$. This observation, combined with the fact that the range of $f$ is the domain of $f^{-1}$, suggests that the inverse of a continuous function is continuous. This result is stated without formal proof.
motivation_md: This concept provides the intuitive geometric basis for understanding why the inverse of a continuous function must also be continuous. By relating the graphical properties of a function and its inverse, it builds a foundation for the formal theorem on the continuity of inverse functions.
recap_md: - The graphs of a one-to-one function $f$ and its inverse $f^{-1}$ are reflections across the line $y=x$.- If $f$ is continuous (has no breaks or holes), its reflection $f^{-1}$ will also be continuous.- This suggests that the inverse of a continuous function is continuous.

title: Theorem 1.6.2: Continuity of Inverse Functions

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

one_liner: If a one-to-one function $f$ is continuous at each point of its domain, then its inverse function $f^{-1}$ is continuous at each point of its domain.
content: If $f$ is a one-to-one function that is continuous at each point of its domain, then its inverse function $f^{-1}$ is continuous at each point of its domain. This means $f^{-1}$ is continuous at each point in the range of $f$.
motivation_md: This theorem formally establishes that the property of continuity is preserved under the operation of taking an inverse for one-to-one functions. This is crucial for analyzing the continuity of inverse trigonometric and logarithmic functions, which are fundamental in higher-level calculus.
recap_md: - If $f$ is a one-to-one function that is continuous on its domain, then $f^{-1}$ is also continuous.- The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$.

title: Theorem 1.6.3: Continuity of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

one_liner: Exponential functions $b^x$ are continuous on $(-\infty, \infty)$ and logarithmic functions $\log_b x$ are continuous on $(0, \infty)$.
content: Let $b>0, b \neq 1$. (a) The function $b^{x}$ is continuous on $(-\infty,+\infty)$. (b) The function $\log _{b} x$ is continuous on $(0,+\infty)$.
motivation_md: This theorem provides fundamental continuity properties for exponential and logarithmic functions, which are essential building blocks for calculus and modeling natural phenomena. Knowing they are continuous allows for direct substitution when evaluating limits within their domains.
recap_md: - Exponential functions $b^x$ (for $b>0, b \neq 1$) are continuous on $(-\infty, \infty)$.- Logarithmic functions $\log_b x$ (for $b>0, b \neq 1$) are continuous on $(0, \infty)$.

title: Obtaining Limits by Squeezing

position.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

one_liner: The method of squeezing proves a limit $f(x) \rightarrow L$ by trapping $f$ between two functions, $g$ and $h$, whose limits are known to be $L$.
content: In Section 1.1, numerical evidence was used to conjecture that $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}=1$.
